items.note: Within-subjects study in two online intro creative writing courses: the same exercise without ChatGPT, with ChatGPT, and with ChatGPT plus instructor guidance, scored by expert judges with the Consensual Assessment Technique; abstract from the white paper PDF does not say whether condition order was randomized, and N = 31 is below the 50 threshold.

Two groups of students prepared weekly materials, one using only AI chatbots and the control using any resource except chatbots; critical thinking and creative skills were reported underdeveloped in the chatbot group, but the abstract does not say how they were scored (essays and conference abstracts were written; student feedback also collected); N = 16.

92 male intermediate EFL learners divided into high-AI-support (LLM writing-assistant feedback), low-AI-support, and conventional-instruction groups, with creative writing pre- and posttests; abstract says 'divided' (one search lane reports computer-generated random assignment in the full text) and does not say whether AI was available at posttest.

40 design students randomly assigned to two groups of 20; in phase 1 one group used a text-to-image tool for an urban furniture design task, in phase 2 both designed without AI; professionals rated outputs on the Creative Product Semantic Scale (authors call it quasi-experimental); has an after_ai phase; N below 50.

Proposes the GPS framework (goals, prompts, strategies) for brainstorming with an LLM and tests it through a design example and a case study, with an adapted TTCT scoring the AI-generated ideas; no comparison condition stated; abstract taken from the arXiv version 2410.11877 of the same work.

SSRN abstract not reachable (403; OpenAlex, Crossref, Semantic Scholar have none); the first author's MSU dissertation summary describes a quasi-experiment in which people wrote with an LLM set to high versus low randomness and the perceived creativity of the work was rated, so it is a likely AI-configuration comparison; check design and N in full text.

Experiment with professional illustrators in which GenAI assistance flattened the quality curve of their artworks and many AI users stopped early; the short SSRN abstract gives neither N nor assignment (search notes cite a university bulletin: 219 artists, 168 randomly allowed GenAI in a second session).

Within-subjects experiment with 62 Chinese university students comparing personalised versus standard GenAI feedback on creative problem-solving (quality and elaboration of solutions) and feedback uptake; an AI-configuration comparison with no no-AI arm; order randomization not stated.

Controlled experiment manipulating the variance of sets of AI-generated design variations and recording which design participants select (aesthetic preference and representativeness tasks); participants judge AI outputs and produce nothing creative, so the outcome is selection, not creativity of their output; borderline because the authors frame it as constrained selection diversity in co-creation; N not stated.

Abstract not reachable (publisher elides it in Semantic Scholar; OpenAlex and Crossref have none; Springer page behind a login redirect); the title describes an empirical study of generative-AI-based creative-thinking training on fine arts students' artistic creativity, and it is included in the Ozkan 2026 meta-analysis; design and comparison group unknown.
